title: Breaking and Entering: Jamie xx
summary: During the Melbourne portion of his Australian tour, Jamie xx joins Simon and Lauren on Breaking and Entering to chat about his latest record In Waves, as well as his collaborators and more.
transcript:
Jamie xx joined Simon Winkler and Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studios on 5 December 2024 during his Australian tour, to discuss his latest album In Waves. A founding member of The xx and a DJ and producer, he combines UK dance music traditions with innovative production techniques. Released nearly a decade after his debut In Colour, In Waves features an array of collaborators and draws on his experience of dance culture around the world.

Host: Welcome back to Australia and to Triple R.

Jamie: Good to be back.

Host: We were delighted the last time you were here to enjoy some guest program selections. We also understand that beyond Triple R, you have some pretty deep connections to Australia, lots of friends here, and increasingly some surfing places you like to go. Is that right?

Jamie: Yeah. I mean, I've been coming here for like 15 years, almost every year, which is great. And I love it, and it kind of feels like a second home sometimes. And I made loads of pals in Melbourne, Sydney and Byron. So we usually manage to do some kind of side party, beach doof thing. Yeah, I love it.

Host: We do want to talk to you a little bit more about the place of surfing in your life at the moment, maybe during the conversation. But perhaps we could begin with In Waves, different kind of waves, of course, your recent album. It came together over a number of years, and we were interested in the story of this record, and maybe the place of patience and allowing things to unfold. Could you talk about that element of the record?

Jamie: Yeah. I mean, I definitely wasn't patient for a long time. And after In Colour, I wanted to make an album pretty much immediately. And I was always making music, and making music with the band and for other people. [Unclear audio at 00:02:54–00:02:56] But I guess just because I'd been doing this for so long and the same thing over and over again, touring, coming to Australia every year, which is all amazing stuff, I think I kind of lost that enjoyment of the making of the music because it was kind of about the end game rather than the process. So I just had to find that again. And during lockdown, I got the chance to go home and be at home for the first time ever, really, for a long period of time. [Unclear audio at 00:03:25–00:03:27] And just started making music again and actually really enjoying it and not thinking about when it would come out, when people would hear it. And it was just such a pleasure.

Host: Jamie, was there a clear point when you started to understand what the album was about and what stories that it would tell, or what story does the album tell?

Jamie: Yeah, I mean, pretty early on, actually, when I started enjoying the music-making process again, the first couple of things I made were 'Dafodil' and 'Breather' from the record. And they both had similar things in them, which was sort of spoken word, and a way that I could get some of my thoughts across without actually having to put my voice in it. And when you're making a record, it's all about finding these sort of limitations that you can work within and then build something from that. So that was a good starting point.

Host: How many songs didn't make it onto the record?

Jamie: So many. But, yeah, I'm very slow in terms of making music, so nothing got finished that didn't make it on the record. And I just spent a long, long time finishing these tracks, and actually the longest time ever tracklisting it, so it felt like a perfect album listen. Because that's still very important to me, even though I think a lot of people don't listen to music that way these days.

Host: I think that's a beautiful thing, to preserve the idea of a sequenced set of songs. We were reading that your friend Kieran Hebden, aka Four Tet, was able to assist you in this process of sequencing the songs. Could you talk a little bit about how he helped you put the puzzle together?

Jamie: Yeah, well, I always try and enlist my friends who I trust to give me some perspective. Especially when you're making a record on your own, it can get to the point where you just lose all perspective and you're just bouncing ideas around in your own head. [Unclear audio at 00:05:28–00:05:31] And I had been playing a lot of these songs out over the years, testing them on crowds, changing things depending on how it was working. So I had an idea of what I wanted to do with the tracklist and then as I was putting it together, [Unclear audio at 00:05:44–00:05:47] I just couldn't get it right because obviously it's totally different to playing a show, even though I kind of worked out an order for live. And Kieran was one of the people who kind of just told me to [Unclear audio at 00:05:56–00:05:59], and it worked.

Host: On that subject, about the idea of songs developing, in some cases in response to audience reactions, could you give us an example of how a song might be adapted based on how an audience reacts?

Jamie: Well, you can really feel it in a room. You can feel the energy levels drop and rise, and also the benefit of being a DJ is I can just stand there and watch them. We've done that as a band with The xx, playing new songs before they've been released, and you're concentrating so hard on just not messing up that you can't really gauge anything except for, like, you know, getting the notes right. So this is, yeah, it was a new way of doing it for me and it's really helpful. And having had all the experience of playing many, many years, yeah, it was a good way of doing it.

[Unclear audio at 00:06:57–00:06:59]

Host: Jamie, today on the show, we're looking back over the year that was 2024, and we wanted to reflect on your own year as well. You hosted a really special event called The Floor. Apparently it's been a bit of a dream of yours for a while to own your own club, ever since you discovered Plastic People, and this year you finally got to fulfil that dream. You had plenty of special guests dropping by, Daphni, John Glacier, Two Shell, Charli xcx, and a whole bunch of others. And you played a set that finished with Light of the World's 'London Town', which is a really lovely jazzy ode to London and its nightlife. Can you tell us a bit more about this night and your intentions for it, and how did it feel to finally have that ambition of The Floor realised?

Jamie: It was really special. I think for a long time I've wanted to own a club, and over the years I've almost bought a couple of spaces to be able to do that in London, and was strongly advised against it by everybody in my life, which I'm grateful for. Because this was only 10 days, but we spent a long time building the space out, making it sound amazing, feel very intimate. And I played 10 nights in a row. And that was enough to satisfy me. It was an incredible experience, extremely exhausting. And then we did it in New York and in LA as well. And just to be able to do that every night and really get your head into it, and also see all your friends and [Unclear audio at 00:08:30–00:08:34] and discover stuff, it was very revitalising after finishing a record.

Host: Your previous album, In Colour, has been described as your nostalgic, rose-tinted homage to a dance floor era that you yourself were too young to experience. Songs like 'Gosh' contain that romance of imagined club experiences and that kind of distant pirate radio signals. Part of the beauty of that record, In Colour, is that it presents a picture of club culture that's through the lens of someone that imagined it before they got to experience it themselves. Are you still able to keep that viewpoint, to romanticise club culture, even though you're more in the centre of it all now?

Jamie: Yeah. I mean, I think the great thing about dance music is that it's always referencing itself and moving so fast. It seems to go in these cycles where people reference 20 years ago and, you know, it's the new kids going to clubs for the first time, starting to make music. They hear that and then do it in a new way, in their own way. And I love that. It's kind of the fastest moving genre of all. But on this album, because I guess I'd been doing it for so long, and also I was just travelling around the world the whole time, I think I wanted to make it less UK-centric and more just based on my experiences of dance floors all over the world.

[Unclear audio at 00:09:56–00:09:58]

Host: We understand that you even sample ambient sounds from different clubs to locate them in particular places. Is that right?

Jamie: Yeah. I mean, it's just a good way to sort of tie things together without anybody noticing as well. It just kind of creates a sort of vibe throughout a record if you just texture it with these sorts of things.

Host: And it does become, as a listener, a very transporting experience. Out of curiosity, as someone who has travelled the world in that environment, in the club culture, are you observing shifts or changes over time? And where would you say things are at that you're experiencing at the moment in club culture?

Jamie: Yeah, it's constantly shifting. And I definitely struggled with it. I mean, I was struggling with making the album at this time anyway. And I think part of it was because dance music, which was this, to me, very personal, special thing that was like the coolest thing in the world when I was a kid, had become basically the biggest thing in the world and was all pop music. And I didn't know where my place was in that. And I felt slightly responsible for it as well. And so I just had to kind of traverse that. And in the end, I basically just stopped listening to dance music for a while and just listened to my old records, my parents' records at home. And that allowed me the headspace to make something that wasn't within the current climate, I guess. [Unclear audio at 00:11:25–00:11:27] And now there's loads of amazing producers making really cool underground music again and I'm learning from them.

Host: And I guess The Floor was a way of platforming and championing those artists as well.

Jamie: Yeah.

Host: Jamie, we were just talking then about also getting in the right headspace. And you've said for most of the time feeling good doesn't necessarily lend itself to making good music, and that you kind of have to separate the two. How are you able to do this? What does it take to get in a music-making frame of mind? What does that look and what does that feel like?

Jamie: I wish I knew. [Unclear audio at 00:12:05–00:12:08] It's always a challenge. [Unclear audio at 00:12:08–00:12:11] I'm a bit older now and can't be going out as much as I used to. And obviously, it's nice to feel good in your body. But also, you do need that inspiration and those moments where you're in a room full of people all listening to the same thing. At least for me, that's super inspiring. So it's all about balance and I'm always trying to find that balance. [Unclear audio at 00:12:33–00:12:35] And it's especially hard when you're on tour. [Unclear audio at 00:12:36–00:12:39] But yeah, I'm working at it always.

Host: Something we were very curious about is the collaborative quality of this record. You're talking about the place of friendship at the heart of In Waves as well. We'd love to talk to you about local heroes, The Avalanches, because of course they feature on the record. You've said that they really helped you, through Since I Left You, their debut, to learn how to make music. You said by listening to that album, you learned so much. How did it feel to create music with The Avalanches all these years later?

Jamie: I mean, it's a dream. I was obsessed with them when I was a kid. When I was like 11, I think that album came out and there wasn't much information about them online. And I was just trawling the internet for anything really, and I went and bought all of the records that they sampled for that and really deep dived on that record. And this was before you could watch tutorials on YouTube about how to make stuff. So I just listened to that and a few other records and worked out how to do it, and that was the basis for how I learned to produce, which was mostly sampling. So then I got to meet them here. They came to one of my shows years ago. I didn't know they were there until afterwards.

Host: That was probably a good thing, right?

Jamie: Yes. I mean, that same show I played a mash-up of a bunch of different tracks from Since I Left You as an ode to them, not knowing they were there, which was kind of embarrassing.

Host: No, I'm sure they appreciated it.

Jamie: But yeah, so working with them has been great, and I think because I learned how to make music by listening to them, when we make music together it just clicks really easily.

Host: What does it look like when you're working together? Did they teach you new techniques and vice versa? Was it a bit of an exchange in that way?

Jamie: It was mostly we would just hang out and talk most of the time, and then when we were doing music it would be separate, and they'd send me little videos of what they were doing on the screen. But it's very little sort of changes to stuff, because everything that they were doing was amazing. So it just worked, you know, it was one of the easiest processes.

[Unclear audio at 00:14:47–00:14:50]

Host: You used a phrase to describe the feeling of a song when you know that it's finished as emotional fullness. How do you define that, and what makes a song emotionally full for you?

[Unclear audio at 00:15:04–00:15:06]

Jamie: I mean, whenever I talk about this, it just sounds—it's a very hard thing to describe. It's basically just a feeling. That's all I can say about it. I try not to overthink it because it's quite a rare thing when I get that feeling. It's actually mostly at the beginning of a track where something happens, usually a mistake, that just makes me feel a certain way where I know that I can turn this into something special.

[Unclear audio at 00:15:33–00:15:36]

Host: I think you've spoken a lot about mistakes being really important. Were there any interesting happy accidents that made their way onto this record?

Jamie: So many. I think most of it's an accident.

Host: It's being open to the creative process and allowing for it to happen.

Jamie: Yes, definitely. Every time I've had an idea and tried to execute it, it's usually pretty dull. But if I just get into that flow state and follow all the mistakes and lose track of time, that's the best.

Host: From your perspective as a producer, it must be interesting to hear the evolution of certain songs too. To use an example, 'Dafodil', we understand, obviously features Panda Bear and John Glacier on the album version, but we understand that there's a 20-minute version floating around there on a hard drive which features some other guest vocalists. Is that right?

Jamie: I mean, a very unfinished 20-minute version, but there's a lot of people that were very kind to deliver verses during lockdown. So it was all via text, and yeah, I'm so grateful to them for all trying. And I'd love to put it together at some point, but that track in particular is very intricate, because it was all to do with chopping these voices up and the rhythm of the vocals. So yeah, it's a long process, and these ones that ended up on the album were just kind of the most different to each other, which I thought was interesting.

Host: Finally, to bring the conversation full circle, we started talking about surfing at the top. We read that you've developed a really strong interest in surfing over the last 10 years. You had an epiphany in Hawaii back in 2014 and haven't looked back. You've said that you love the trippy, spiritual vibe of surf culture. Can you tell us more about that? And I'm wondering, does surfing culture offer a shift in perspective for you?

Jamie: Yeah, well, I think it's just the exact opposite to anything I do professionally, which is perfect for me. And I think that I discovered it when I was 25, and it felt like just an incredible thing to have a brand new passion at that point in life, when I thought my whole life was about music before that. I was a city kid, so I wasn't interested in nature at all. And it just flipped everything, and now any chance I get, I'll go to a spot.

Host: So hopefully there'll be some time on this tour.

Jamie: Yeah, I'm going to hopefully get some surfing in Sydney and then going to Byron for a few days, and that'd be great.

Host: Thanks for joining us, Jamie.

Jamie: Thank you.
